Oregon LEA: the study plan

LEA is Oregon's Limited Energy Technician license, Class A: the license for limited-energy systems such as fire alarm, security, access control, video and data. This hub is practice; the licensing exam, eligibility and hours are set by the Oregon Building Codes Division (BCD).

Before you start

  1. Confirm the current eligibility, hours, fees and exam scheduling with Oregon BCD. They change; the hub does not track them.
  2. Tell Provider Services you are on the LEA path so Compliance can confirm your hours and paperwork.
  3. Get the code books the exam allows, in the editions Oregon currently adopts.

Start with the instructor course set

The Instructor course set domain is the LEA course built by our licensed Oregon instructor: OAR and ORS rules, NEC questions, voltage drop math, flash cards and color codes. Drill it first, then widen to the full bank.

Four weeks, one hour a day

Week 1Oregon LEA rules: licensing, scope, permits, inspection, penalties, continuing education. Flash cards daily.
Week 2NEC for limited energy: Articles 90, 110, 250, 300, 725, 760, 770, 800 to 840. Take a 25-question domain test each day.
Week 3Fire alarm and security, access, video and data. Calculations every other day with the Calculator tab.
Week 4Full 100-question mixed exams, then Retest my misses until misses are rare. Stop when you score well above the passing mark three times in a row.

Test-day habits

  • Answer the ones you know first; flag and come back.
  • For code questions, find the article first, then the section; do not answer from memory when you can look it up.
  • Read every option. "All of the above" and "except" questions catch people who stop at the first good answer.
  • Do the math on paper and check the units.

License and certification blocks

  • Questions tied to one state's license or one certification (Oregon LEA, NICET 1, a state license) live only in their own block. They never appear in the SSU assessment, the level exams or the exam bank.
  • NICET 1 is the Level 3 and Level 4 fire path; the FA specialty needs NICET 1 at minimum.
  • States and cities adopt code editions on their own schedule, and some still enforce older NEC or NFPA editions. Study the edition your AHJ adopted; Compliance confirms it.
  • NEC, low-voltage and CAT 1 questions that are not tied to one license stay in the general tests.

Assessments and leveling

  • SSU assessment: 50 questions from the approved SSU bank, all subjects. Use it as a baseline before training and again after.
  • Level exams L1 to L4: the AAASSU level exams from the Tech Leveling Framework: L1 Foundation (IN1 / SV1), L2 Residential Pro (IN2 / SV2), L3 Unity Pro (IN3 / SV3), L4 Commercial Pro (IN4 / SV4). Pass mark 80%. Your level is set by course completion and field sign-off (0 not completed, 1 completed, 2 field tested, 3 training to train, 4 trainer); the exam score is one part of it; vendor courses, certifications and sign-offs complete it, and your trainer and Provider Services confirm it.
  • Every score saves to your training record automatically.

The AAA exam bank

  • 242 questions in 17 subjects, each tagged critical, high or medium. Start with Critical only, then work subject by subject.
  • The Glossary (definitions and key fire alarm terms) is in Flash cards and Study cards.
  • The Licensing questions in this bank are written for Illinois (IDFPR). Use them as practice only; your state's rules come from your licensing board and Compliance.

Using the hub

  • Tests: pick the bank, domain and length. Explanations show after you submit, and Retest my misses builds a test from what you got wrong.
  • Flash cards: tap to flip; Got it removes the card, Again puts it back a few cards later. Finish and save records the session.
  • Study cards: search any word (for example "ground" or "725") to see every related question with its answer and the why.
  • My results: your history and best score by test on this phone.

Calculator

Quick field math for study and the job. Check every result against the code edition your AHJ enforces.

Ohm's law and power

Enter any two; leave the others blank.

Voltage drop (two-wire DC or single-phase)

VD = 2 × K × I × L ÷ CM. K is about 12.9 for copper, 21.2 for aluminum.

Battery amp-hours

Standby amps × standby hours, plus alarm amps × alarm minutes ÷ 60. Add the safety margin and durations your code edition and AHJ require.
